requirements: The core contributions of the paper 'vAttention: Dynamic Memory Management for Serving LLMs without PagedAttention' have been reproduced, including the vAttention memory manager built atop CUDA VMM APIs, extensions to NVIDIA drivers for sub-2MB page-groups, integration with FlashAttention-2/FlashInfer/FA3/vLLM inside a vLLM-based serving framework, and the prefill/decode/end-to-end/ablation results on Yi-6B, Llama-3-8B and Yi-34B.

The motivating measurements demonstrating PagedAttention overhead — prefill slowdown of FA2/FlashInfer paged vs non-paged kernels (Figure 2), vLLM decode kernel sensitivity to block size (Figure 3), and the qualitative CPU/GPU overheads called out in Section 3 and Table 1 — are reproduced.

The Figure-2 harness sweeps context lengths {1K, 2K, 4K, 8K, 16K, 32K} tokens on Llama-3-8B on a single A100, executing all four configurations (FA2 non-paged, FA2 paged, FlashInfer non-paged, FlashInfer paged) with warm-up plus a fixed number of timed repetitions per point.

Measured: on Llama-3-8B / 1×A100, the FA2 paged prefill kernel is up to ~37% slower than the FA2 non-paged prefill kernel across context lengths 1K–32K (Figure 2 headline: max overhead ≈ 1.37×).

Measured: on Llama-3-8B / 1×A100, the FlashInfer paged prefill kernel is up to ~42% slower than the FlashInfer non-paged prefill kernel across context lengths 1K–32K (Figure 2 headline: max overhead ≈ 1.42×).
Figure 3 (sensitivity of vLLM's paged decode kernel latency to KV-cache block size) is reproduced on Llama-3-8B / 1×A100.

The Figure-3 harness sweeps (batch_size × context_length) points {1×16K, 2×16K, 4×16K, 8×16K, 16×16K} with per-request context length fixed at 16K tokens.

Measured: for vLLM's paged decode kernel on Llama-3-8B / 1×A100, changing the KV-cache block size can change kernel execution time by up to ~1.9× (Figure 3 / Table 1 headline: max block-size sensitivity ≈ 1.90×).

Measured: at the largest sweep point (16×16K) the block-128 to block-16 latency ratio for vLLM's paged decode kernel is ≈1.90× (matching the value annotated on Figure 3), with block-64 also showing >1.4× overhead over block-16.
Section 3.3.1 GPU-side runtime overhead analysis of PagedAttention kernels (extra instructions and register pressure) is reproduced.

Code has been implemented that provides a Nsight-Compute (ncu) / nvprof profiling script which extracts total executed-instruction counts and register-usage statistics for paged and non-paged attention kernel launches of FA2 and FlashInfer.
Measured: the number of executed instructions in the PagedAttention prefill kernels of FA2 and FlashInfer is 7–13% higher than in the corresponding non-paged kernels (Section 3.3.1 headline).

Measured: profiling of the PagedAttention kernels reports register spilling (nonzero stack-frame / spill-store bytes) that is absent in the non-paged counterparts, corroborating the paper's claim that caching page indices increases register pressure and causes spills.

The vAttention library implementation is functionally correct: pre-reservation of 2N contiguous virtual tensors sized B*L*H*D*P per worker, per-request reqId sub-tensor indexing, integration with the PyTorch caching allocator via 'virtual tensors', and the init/alloc_reqid/free_reqid/step API contract (Table 4, Algorithm 1) that wraps CUDA VMM APIs.

Pre-reservation of contiguous virtual memory buffers for the KV cache (Section 5.1.1–5.1.3): the library allocates 2N virtual tensors per worker of size B*S = B*L*H*D*P and defers all physical memory commitment.

Code has been implemented such that per worker the library reserves exactly 2*N virtual memory buffers, where N is the number of transformer layers hosted on that worker (one buffer for the K cache and one for the V cache per layer).

Code has been implemented such that each reserved virtual buffer has size BS = B * S where S = L * H * D * P (maximum batch size × maximum context length × KV heads per worker × head dimension × bytes per element), as defined in Section 5.1.3.

Code has been implemented such that immediately after init() completes, the reserved virtual buffers have no physical memory mapped into them (physical pages are only allocated separately and only mapped later by step()).

Code has been implemented such that the 2N virtual buffers are reserved for the lifetime of the serving application (never freed and re-reserved between requests), matching the behavior described at the top of Section 5.3.1.

For the Yi-34B TP-2 worked example in Section 5.1.3 (N=60, H=4, D=128, P=2, L=200K, B=500), the per-worker single-buffer size S equals 200 MB, per-buffer size BS equals 100 GB, and total per-worker virtual reservation across 120 buffers equals 12 TB, matching the paper's numbers.
PyTorch caching allocator extension enabling 'virtual tensors' (Section 5.2.2, Figure 6): tensors that occupy reserved virtual memory but have no physical backing until later mapping.

Code has been implemented that extends the PyTorch caching allocator so that a tensor can be reserved in virtual memory without cudaMalloc committing physical memory (i.e., a virtual-tensor allocation path that does not go through the standard cudaMalloc-backed caching allocator).

Code has been implemented such that the KV cache tensors returned to the serving framework are ordinary torch.Tensor objects with the requested shape and dtype (so unmodified attention kernels can consume them), but no physical GPU pages are consumed until step() maps them.

Code has been implemented such that all non-KV-cache memory objects (activations, weights, workspace) continue to go through the standard PyTorch caching allocator / cudaMalloc path, and only the KV cache is routed through the vAttention virtual-tensor path (Figure 6).

Per-request reqId sub-tensor indexing scheme (Section 5.2.3): each active request occupies a non-overlapping [reqId*S, (reqId+1)*S) slice of every virtual buffer, keyed by an integer reqId in [0, B-1].
Code has been implemented such that reqId values allocated by the library are integers strictly in the range [0, B-1], where B is the maximum batch size configured via init().

Code has been implemented such that the K cache (or V cache) sub-tensor of a request within a virtual buffer starts at byte offset reqId * S, where S = L * H * D * P is the maximum per-layer K (or V) cache size of a single request on the worker.

Code has been implemented such that at any point in time, distinct active reqIds address non-overlapping sub-regions of the virtual buffers (verified by inspecting the (offset, length) pairs used to map physical pages).

vAttention wraps the low-level CUDA virtual memory management (VMM) APIs listed in Table 3, exposing a matching v* API surface (vMemReserve, vMemCreate, vMemMap, vMemRelease, vMemFree) that internally calls the CUDA driver primitives.
Code has been implemented such that vMemReserve reserves a virtual-memory buffer by invoking (directly or via the patched driver) the cuMemAddressReserve primitive, per Table 3 row 1.
Code has been implemented such that vMemCreate allocates a physical-memory handle by invoking the cuMemCreate primitive (or its patched-driver equivalent for sub-2MB pages), per Table 3 row 2.

Code has been implemented such that a single call to vMemMap performs both mapping (cuMemMap) and access enablement (cuMemSetAccess), combining the two CUDA calls into one API as described in Section 6.2.

Code has been implemented such that a single call to vMemRelease performs both unmapping (cuMemUnmap) and physical-handle release (cuMemRelease), combining the two CUDA calls into one API as described in Section 6.2.
Code has been implemented such that vMemFree releases a virtual-memory buffer by invoking cuMemAddressFree (or its patched-driver equivalent), per Table 3 row 7.

Code has been implemented such that vMemCreate/vMemMap accept a page-group size (64KB / 128KB / 256KB / 2MB) and enforce that both the virtual buffer size and the physical handle size are multiples of that page-group size, matching Section 5.2.1's granularity constraint.
Measured latency of a single vMemMap call for a 64KB page-group is approximately 8 microseconds on the target A100 host, matching Table 3's vMemMap 64KB entry.

Measured latency of a single cuMemMap plus cuMemSetAccess pair for a 2MB page is approximately 46 microseconds (8 + 38) on the target A100 host, matching Table 3's cuMemMap/cuMemSetAccess 2MB entries and the ~40μs figure cited in Section 6.1.
The init API (Table 4 row 1) initializes vAttention with the model geometry (N, B, L, H, D, P) plus a page-group size, and returns the list of KV cache tensors to the serving framework.

Code has been implemented such that init() accepts exactly the arguments N (num layers), B (max batch), L (max context length), H (KV heads per worker), D (head dim), P (bytes per element), and page-group-size, matching Table 4.

Code has been implemented such that init() returns a Python list of 2*N torch.Tensor handles (K cache and V cache per layer), each of shape [B, L, H, D] with the configured dtype, ready to be consumed by attention kernels.

Code has been implemented such that init() also pre-allocates a pool of physical page-groups on the worker (via vMemCreate) but does not map them into any KV cache buffer, matching Section 5.3.1's 'pre-allocates physical memory pages at each worker during initialization' behavior.
The alloc_reqid API (Table 4 row 2, Algorithm 1 line 8) hands out an unused reqId and marks it active.
Code has been implemented such that alloc_reqid() takes no arguments and returns a single integer in [0, B-1], matching Table 4.

Code has been implemented such that alloc_reqid selects a reqId that is not currently active (or that is available for deferred re-use per Section 6.1.2), marks it active, and never returns the same value to two live requests concurrently.
The free_reqid API (Table 4 row 3, Algorithm 1 line 19) marks a reqId inactive; physical memory may or may not be reclaimed immediately depending on the deferred-reclamation policy.
Code has been implemented such that free_reqid takes exactly one integer argument (the reqId) and returns None, matching Table 4.
Code has been implemented such that after free_reqid(id) returns, the reqId no longer counts as active and its slot becomes available for a subsequent alloc_reqid() call.

The step API (Table 4 row 4, Algorithm 1 line 13) guarantees that every active reqId has enough physical page-groups mapped to cover its current context length before model.forward runs, and reports success or failure.

Code has been implemented such that step accepts a length-B array/tensor of per-slot context lengths (with 0 for inactive reqIds) and returns 0 on success or -1 on out-of-memory / mapping failure, matching Table 4.

Code has been implemented such that when step returns 0, every active reqId has ceil(context_length * per-token-bytes / t) page-groups mapped in each of the 2N virtual buffers (where t is the configured page-group size), covering the full current context length.

Code has been implemented such that for a request in the prefill phase with per-layer K-cache prompt-size s and page-group size t, step maps at least ceil((s + t - 1) / t) page-groups into each of the 2N virtual buffers for that reqId, matching the formula in Section 5.3.3.

Code has been implemented such that for a request already in the decode phase, step maps at most one additional page-group per virtual buffer per invocation (since one iteration produces at most one new token), matching Section 5.3.3.

Code has been implemented such that vAttention internally tracks, for each reqId, how many page-groups are currently mapped in each virtual buffer, and only issues new vMemMap calls when the existing mapping is about to be exhausted (not on every step call).

Code has been implemented such that when the physical page pool is exhausted and step cannot satisfy the requested mapping, it returns -1 (failure) rather than raising an exception or silently proceeding, matching Table 4 and enabling framework-level preemption per Section 5.3.3.
The serving-framework integration follows Algorithm 1: per-iteration loop of alloc_reqid → update cache_seq_len → step → model.forward → increment cache_seq_len or free_reqid on completion.

Code has been implemented such that the scheduler's main loop mirrors Algorithm 1 lines 6–24 (iterate over new_requests, then step(cache_seq_len), then model.forward, then iterate over active_requests to update or free), rather than an ad-hoc order.

Code has been implemented such that when a new request is admitted (can_schedule returns True), the scheduler calls vattention.alloc_reqid() and records the returned index in req_batch_idx[R_i], matching Algorithm 1 lines 7–10.

Code has been implemented such that cache_seq_len[idx] is set to prompt_len(R_i) when a request is first scheduled and incremented by 1 in every subsequent decode iteration until completion, matching Algorithm 1 lines 10 and 22.

Code has been implemented such that vattention.step(cache_seq_len) is called immediately before model.forward() every iteration, and forward is not launched if step returned failure, matching Algorithm 1 lines 13–14.
Code has been implemented such that when is_complete(R_i) becomes true, the scheduler sets cache_seq_len[idx] = 0 and calls vattention.free_reqid(idx), matching Algorithm 1 lines 17–19.

Code has been implemented such that when step returns -1 (out-of-memory), the scheduler preempts one or more running requests (freeing their reqIds) and retries, matching the fallback behavior described at the end of Section 5.3.3.

Support for continuous batching with 'holes' in the virtual batch dimension caused by mid-batch exits (end of Section 5.3.4): Q and KV cache may have different batch orderings and vAttention uses FlashAttention's cache_batch_idx to reconnect them.

Code has been implemented such that when a request is dispatched to the attention kernel, its cache_batch_idx argument is set to its reqId so that the compact Q batch dimension (indexed 0..batch_active-1) is mapped to the correct sparse KV-cache slot.

Code has been implemented such that when a request in the middle of the running batch exits, vAttention does NOT physically move any surviving request's KV cache; the hole is left in place and cache_batch_idx of the remaining requests is updated to preserve their existing KV-cache locations.

Section 6.1 optimizations are implemented in the step API: overlap of physical-memory mapping with model compute in the decode phase using a background thread, deferred reclamation of finished reqIds, and eager allocation of page-groups for an inactive reqId to hide prefill allocation latency.

The decode-phase optimization overlaps CUDA VMM physical-memory mapping with model compute via a background thread spawned by the step API, exploiting the per-iteration predictability of decode memory demand.

Code has been implemented so that the step API launches a background worker thread (rather than performing all memory mapping synchronously on the calling thread) when it detects that upcoming decode iterations will require additional page-group mappings.

Code has been implemented so that vAttention maintains, per active reqId, both the current context length and the number of physical page-groups already mapped into each of the 2N virtual KV cache tensors.

Code has been implemented so that during iteration i-1 the library computes which requests will exhaust their currently mapped page-groups in iteration i, and schedules the mapping work for iteration i on the background thread.

The decode-phase code path allocates at most one new page-group per virtual KV tensor per active decode request per iteration, matching the invariant that a decode iteration produces one output token per request.

Code has been implemented so that the background thread issues the CUDA VMM mapping calls (cuMemMap + cuMemSetAccess for 2MB pages, or the equivalent vMemMap for sub-2MB page-groups) rather than the compute thread.

The compute-thread step API path does not block on the mapping work being performed on the background thread when the mapping is being prepared for a future iteration (i.e., pre-mapping never stalls the current iteration's kernel launch).

The Figure 12 trace is reproduced: with overlapping enabled, per-decode-iteration latency for the described Llama-3-8B configuration (batch size 32, per-request prefill context 2K–3K, 2MB pages) is flat, whereas synchronous allocation shows recurring 5–15 ms latency spikes tied to iterations that require new page-groups.

Deferred reclamation retains a completed request's physical page-groups so that a subsequently-arriving request can inherit its reqId (and thus its already-mapped KV cache tensor sub-regions), avoiding CUDA VMM allocation calls on the prefill critical path.
Code has been implemented so that free_reqid marks the reqId inactive but does not immediately unmap the physical pages backing its KV cache sub-tensors.
Code has been implemented that maintains a pool/cache of reclaimable but still-mapped page-groups belonging to freed reqIds, distinct from the pool of unmapped physical handles.

Eager allocation proactively maps a small number of page-groups into the virtual tensors of one inactive reqId so that the next arriving prefill request can start execution without any critical-path CUDA VMM calls.

Code has been implemented so that upon a new-request arrival, alloc_reqid hands out the pre-warmed reqId, then the library selects a new inactive reqId and schedules eager mapping of page-groups into its virtual tensors.
The eager pre-mapping work is executed on the step API's background thread, not on the compute thread, so it does not stall ongoing iterations.

For a request whose prefill fits within the eagerly-mapped page-groups, the prefill critical path contains zero CUDA VMM allocation calls (verifiable by counting driver invocations during a prefill iteration).

The number of page-groups kept pre-mapped per inactive reqId (and the threshold below which reclamation triggers) is configurable via the vAttention initialization or a runtime knob rather than a hard-coded literal deep in the code.
The step API (Section 5.3) implements the contract that ties the three latency-hiding optimizations to the serving framework's per-iteration control flow.

The step API accepts an array of length B (max batch size) containing the current context length of every reqId, with 0 indicating an inactive slot, matching the signature described in Table 4 and Algorithm 1.
The step API returns 0 on success and -1 on failure (insufficient physical memory to satisfy the requested mappings), as specified in Table 4.

For a prefill scheduled in the current iteration with per-layer per-tensor K cache size s and page-group size t, step ensures that at least ceil((s + t - 1) / t) page-groups are mapped in each of the 2N virtual tensors of that reqId before returning success.

step synchronizes with the background thread (waiting for any mappings needed for the current iteration to complete) before returning control to the compute thread, guaranteeing kernel launches see valid physical backing.

The serving framework integration reacts to a -1 return from step by preempting one or more active requests to allow forward progress, matching vLLM's default preemption behavior described in Section 5.3.3.

Setting cache_seq_len[idx] = 0 for a reqId in the array passed to step is treated as marking that slot inactive for the iteration, so no mapping work is scheduled for it (consistent with Algorithm 1 lines 17-19 and the deferred-reclamation policy).
